Immigration to the United States—the mass arrival of millions of people seeking economic opportunity, political freedom, and escape from hardship—transformed America from a nation of four million in 1790 to over three hundred million by the late twentieth century. Between 1840 and 1920, roughly thirty-five million people entered the United States, predominantly from Europe. Subsequent waves brought Asians, Latin Americans, and Africans. Ellis Island, operating from 1892 to 1954, became the symbolic gateway, processing over twelve million immigrants. The phenomenon reshaped American culture, labour markets, and politics while generating persistent nativism and legal restriction.

Early waves from the 1840s to the 1880s were predominantly Irish and German, fleeing famine and political upheaval. They faced discrimination but assimilated within two generations. The so-called "new immigration" from the 1880s to 1924 brought Italians, Poles, Jews, and others from southern and eastern Europe. They clustered in industrial cities, maintaining ethnic communities and languages longer than northern Europeans. Anti-Chinese sentiment led to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the first explicit U.S. law barring an ethnic group, with similar exclusions following afterward.

Most immigrants were economic migrants seeking factory work, land ownership, or better conditions. Push factors included industrialization, land scarcity, and pogroms in Europe and Asia. Nativism—the fear that immigrants threatened American culture and wages—drove the Immigration Act of 1924, which imposed strict national-origin quotas favouring northern Europeans and cutting immigration to a trickle. The quota system lasted until 1965. Subsequent immigration has been more diverse globally and legalized through specialized categories such as work, family, and refugee visas. Immigration remains central to American self-mythology as the nation of immigrants despite legal restrictions, and debates over immigration define contemporary politics.
